strengths: Addresses a timely and important safety issue: inadvertent geolocation-based privacy leakage from agentic multimodal reasoning models (ChatGPT o3), which is distinct from prior work on training-data memorization or landmark-based geolocation.
Realistic and creative threat scenario: casual selfies in front of private residences rather than tourist landmarks, which is a meaningful shift from prior privacy-leakage benchmarks.

Provides a clue taxonomy (building features, identification markers, urban infrastructure, property features, urban planning) that could be useful for future privacy-risk analysis and for designing obfuscation countermeasures.

Illustrative qualitative transcripts (Figures 7-13) give readers good intuition for how the model chains web search, image analysis, and reasoning to infer addresses, which is compelling as a case study demonstration.
Clear, well-motivated writing and figures; the paper is easy to follow and the risk it highlights is societally relevant.
weaknesses: Extremely small dataset (only 50 images), manually curated by the authors without a documented, reproducible sampling protocol, which severely limits the statistical reliability of reported percentages (60% within 1 mile, 84% within 5 miles).

Only a single proprietary model (ChatGPT o3) is evaluated; there is no comparison with other MLLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude with tool use) to establish whether this is o3-specific or a general capability of agentic MLLMs, undermining the generality of the claims.

The occlusion/masking 'causal' experiments supporting claims about critical visual clues rely on only 2-3 anecdotal examples (Figures 10-13) rather than a systematic, quantitative ablation across the dataset; conclusions about which clue categories matter most are largely derived from frequency counts of self-reported model reasoning traces, a weak proxy for actual causal contribution.

No human baseline is measured, despite the paper repeatedly claiming the identified cues 'would be difficult for regular human inspectors' to notice, leaving this central comparative claim unsubstantiated.

The dataset cannot be released due to Street View licensing, and detailed collection/annotation protocols (e.g., inter-annotator agreement for clue labeling, criteria for image selection) are not provided, harming reproducibility.
No proposed or systematically evaluated defense/mitigation method; the paper only gestures at obfuscation as 'one possible direction' without evaluating its effectiveness at scale.

The formal problem statement (Eq. 1) is a generic autoregressive decomposition that adds little insight beyond standard notation; overall the paper leans heavily on case-study narrative rather than rigorous quantitative methodology.

Ethical/IRB considerations around collecting and analyzing images of real individuals' homes and inferred daily activity patterns (even with blurred faces) are only briefly addressed, without discussion of consent scope, data handling, or review board approval.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important societal concern: inadvertent geolocation-based privacy leakage from agentic multimodal reasoning models (ChatGPT o3) that combine visual reasoning with web search/tool use.

The qualitative case studies (Figures 7-13) are illustrative and provide an intuitive, concrete demonstration of how chain-of-thought reasoning plus web search can triangulate location from subtle visual cues (street layout, signage, architectural details).

The clue taxonomy (Figure 14) categorizing visual cues into building features, identification markers, urban infrastructure, property features, and urban planning is a reasonable organizing scheme that could be useful for future privacy-auditing work.

The occlusion/masking experiments, although limited, provide some causal evidence that specific visual elements (e.g., a distinctive cross, signage) drive geolocation accuracy, moving beyond purely correlational clue-frequency analysis.
weaknesses: Extremely small dataset: only 50 manually collected images, which is far too small to support the paper's headline statistical claims (e.g., '60% within 1 mile,' '84% within 5 miles') with any reasonable confidence or statistical significance; no confidence intervals, variance, or robustness checks are reported.

No baseline or comparative evaluation: the study examines only ChatGPT o3 and does not benchmark against other agentic/multimodal models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, open-source VLMs) to show whether this is a model-specific or a general capability/risk, undermining claims about the novelty and generality of the finding.

Clue identification and categorization appear to be done manually/subjectively by the authors reading model outputs, with no inter-annotator agreement, reliability check, or quantitative validation of the clue taxonomy — this weakens the 'clue analysis' findings (Figures 4-5).

The occlusion/masking 'causal' experiments are only demonstrated on a handful of qualitative examples (2-3 cases in the appendix) rather than systematically across the dataset, so the claim that occlusion 'causally demonstrates' reduced accuracy is not rigorously supported at scale.

No proposed or evaluated defense/mitigation mechanism beyond noting that masking a single clue is often insufficient when redundant clues exist; the paper identifies a risk but offers no technical contribution toward solving it (e.g., no training-time or inference-time mitigation method, no evaluation of existing privacy-preserving techniques).

Methodological contribution is thin: the paper is essentially a descriptive red-teaming/case study with a small manually curated dataset and prompt engineering (4 prompt variants), rather than a new technique, benchmark with broad coverage, or theoretical analysis; this limits its significance for a top-tier AI venue.

Ethical considerations are underexplored: the dataset contains real individuals (faces blurred) and real private residences sourced from Google Maps; while the paper states the dataset won't be released, it is unclear whether proper consent/IRB-like review was obtained for collecting and analyzing identifiable real-world private locations and depicted individuals, which is an important issue for a paper centered on privacy harm.

Lack of statistical rigor in 'Distance Analysis': the paper reports simple percentages from n=50 without any discussion of sampling bias (e.g., overrepresentation of major U.S. cities, selection of especially 'leak-prone' scenes), which likely inflates the apparent severity and generalizability of the risk.

The related work and framing claim to be 'the first' systematic study of geolocation privacy leakage in agentic MLRMs, but several cited works (e.g., [15]-[17], [29]) already study geolocation privacy risks in VLMs; the distinction drawn (tourist/landmark vs. casual selfie scenes) is relatively narrow and the novelty claim may be overstated.

No human baseline comparison is quantitatively established (the paper only asserts that cues are 'difficult for regular human inspectors' without a controlled human study), weakening the comparative claim that the model's capability represents a meaningfully new risk beyond what motivated humans could already do with available OSINT tools.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored privacy risk: inference-time geolocation leakage from agentic multimodal reasoning models with tool-calling capabilities, distinct from prior training-data-memorization privacy work.
The threat scenario (casual selfies with private residences/background elements, rather than tourist landmark photos) is realistic and more concerning than prior geolocation-privacy benchmarks.
Provides a fine-grained taxonomy of visual clues (5 categories, ~25 sub-clue types) with frequency analysis, offering interpretability into which visual elements drive successful inference.

Includes targeted occlusion/masking experiments that causally demonstrate the contribution of specific clues (e.g., masking a distinctive cross reduces precision from address-level to city-level), which is a nice controlled complement to the correlational clue-frequency analysis.

Rich qualitative case studies (full reasoning traces in the appendix) make the model's tool-use behavior (web search, image cropping/zooming) transparent and illustrate the mechanism of leakage convincingly.
weaknesses: The dataset is very small (only 50 images), which limits statistical reliability of the reported percentages (60% within 1 mile, 84% within 5 miles) and the clue-frequency rankings; no confidence intervals or variance across repeated queries are reported.

Only a single model (ChatGPT o3) is evaluated. Without comparison to other frontier agentic/tool-using MLLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude with browsing), it is unclear whether this is a general risk of agentic MLLMs or specific to o3, undermining the paper's broader claims about 'agentic multi-modal large reasoning models' as a class.

No human baseline is empirically measured (only an informal claim that clues are 'difficult for regular human inspectors'); a controlled human geolocation study would substantially strengthen the central privacy-risk claim.

Clue categorization/annotation appears to be done manually by the authors with no reported inter-annotator agreement or validation, raising concerns about subjectivity in the clue-frequency and category analyses.

The masking/occlusion experiments are shown only as a couple of qualitative case studies rather than a systematic, quantified experiment across the dataset (e.g., accuracy drop under masking for all 50 images), which weakens the strength of the causal claims.

Ethical considerations around constructing a dataset of real, identifiable private residences (with real people, only faces blurred) for a privacy-leakage study are not thoroughly discussed (e.g., consent of photographed individuals/homeowners, IRB approval, or a broader responsible-disclosure protocol beyond not releasing images/dataset).

The paper is primarily a red-teaming/evaluation study without a proposed or evaluated defense mechanism beyond a brief note that obfuscating key clues can reduce (but not eliminate) leakage; this limits the paper's contribution to characterization rather than mitigation.

Prompt design (4 prompt variants) is ad hoc and the criterion for selecting 'the highest precision as final prediction' across prompts is not well justified methodologically, potentially inflating the reported leakage rate versus a single fixed, realistic prompt.

strengths: Addresses a novel and increasingly pressing risk (location-related privacy leakage via MLRM reasoning) that is largely absent from current model safety reports and prior geolocation-privacy benchmarks.

DOXBENCH dataset is a meaningful contribution: high-resolution, self-collected images spanning three explicitly defined privacy risk levels (including a novel 'Mirror'/reflection category), addressing the low-resolution/public-landmark bias of prior datasets.
Broad and systematic evaluation spanning 11 models (MLRMs and MLLMs, open- and closed-source), multiple prompting strategies (vanilla, CoT), and Top-1/Top-3 settings.

Careful, multi-pronged root-cause analysis (human evaluation + LLM-as-judge for clue-based reasoning, CLUEMINER clue categorization, tool-augmented reasoning, mirror-case study) that converges on a coherent causal story.
GEOMINER attack framework and the human-vs-model comparison study provide credible evidence of real-world attack feasibility and lowered barriers for non-expert adversaries.
Defense analysis (image perturbation, prompt-based, guardrail-based) is thorough and honestly reports failure modes rather than overselling defenses, adding practical value.
Proposes new evaluation metrics (VRR, GLARE) attempting a more principled accounting of both response rate and localization precision instead of relying on a single distance metric.
weaknesses: The human comparison study is very small (5 undergraduate students, 30 images), limiting the statistical robustness of claims like '15-21x lower error than humans'.

GLARE metric, while framed with an elaborate information-theoretic derivation, rests on several somewhat arbitrary modeling choices (uniform land prior, geometric mean of median/mean error, flat-earth approximation) whose practical validity or correlation with perceived privacy harm is not empirically validated against human judgment.

Dataset images are staged/self-captured by the researchers (posed selfies, driven scenarios) rather than genuine user-generated social media content, which somewhat undercuts the paper's own critique of prior work's lack of ecological validity.
Dataset is geographically restricted to California, raising questions about generalizability of findings (architectural styles, signage, etc.) to other regions/countries.

Reproducibility and release plan for DOXBENCH are unclear given its privacy-sensitive nature (real GPS coordinates/EXIF data), which could limit community verification or itself pose a dual-use risk if released.
Numeric comparisons (percentage gains, GLARE differences) are reported extensively without confidence intervals or variance across runs, weakening the statistical rigor of claims.

Some overlap in novelty with existing geolocation-privacy/VLM-as-GeoGuessr works; the core capability demonstration (MLRMs can geolocate from subtle clues) is incremental relative to concurrent work, with the main new contributions being the dataset, metric, and attack framework rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon.
Presentation contains minor inconsistencies (e.g., unexplained bolding in Table 1) and dense jargon (CLUEMINER, GEOMINER, GLARE) that could be streamlined for clarity.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: inference-time geolocation privacy leakage from MLRMs/MLLMs, as opposed to the more commonly studied training-data memorization privacy risks.

Introduces DoxBench, a purpose-built dataset with three privacy risk levels and EXIF ground truth, attempting to move beyond the low-resolution/iconic-landmark datasets used in prior GeoGuessr-style work.
Broad empirical coverage: 11 models (open- and closed-source, MLRMs and MLLMs), Top-1/Top-3 settings, CoT ablations, tool-augmented reasoning, and a human-vs-model comparison.
Attempts a more nuanced evaluation protocol (VRR, hierarchical census-based accuracy, and the composite GLARE metric) rather than relying on a single error-distance number.
Includes a defense discussion (noise perturbation, prompt-based refusal, guardrail models) that honestly reports largely negative/inconsistent results rather than overselling a fix.
The 'Mirror' category and CLUEMINER/GEOMINER analyses provide some interpretability into which visual clue types drive leakage.
weaknesses: Ecological validity of the dataset is questionable: images are staged/posed by the researchers themselves in California only, not genuine user-generated social media content, undermining the central claim that this better reflects 'real-world' leakage than prior Street-View/landmark datasets.

The human baseline study uses only 5 undergraduate CS students and 30 images, a very small and non-representative sample for the paper's strong claims about 'non-expert humans' and the 15–21x gap; no statistical testing or variance is reported.

The GLARE metric is overly complex and relies on multiple strong, under-justified assumptions (uniform land prior, flat-Earth approximation, geometric mean of median/mean error) without any validation that it tracks real perceived privacy risk better than simpler metrics; its behavior (e.g., ranking an open-source model with poor fine-grained accuracy as 'riskier' via high VRR) raises concerns that the metric rewards verbosity/confidence over actual precision.

Limited methodological novelty: CoT prompting, LLM-as-judge clue categorization, and a two-stage detector/analyzer pipeline (GeoMiner) are mostly straightforward applications of existing techniques (CoT, agentic pipelines) rather than new algorithmic contributions.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-run variance reported anywhere in Table 1 or subsequent experiments, despite LLM outputs being stochastic, weakening confidence in fine-grained numerical comparisons across 11 models and two settings.

The defense section yields essentially all-negative results without proposing or validating any genuinely effective mitigation, leaving the 'solution' contribution of the paper thin; the future-directions section is speculative rather than demonstrated.

Dual-use/ethical concerns are only lightly addressed: the paper essentially documents and refines an attack recipe (including recreating a real stalking/assault case) with GEOMINER and tool-augmented O3, but the ethical statement focuses mainly on image collection consent rather than the broader risk of publishing a ready-made attack blueprint.

Reliance on closed-source, frequently-updated commercial APIs (OpenAI o3, Gemini, Claude) raises reproducibility concerns, since reported numbers may not be stable or reproducible as these models change over time.

Some claims in the text (e.g., 'first to explicitly define location-related privacy leakage from images') are strong relative to clearly related concurrent/prior work already cited (e.g., refs [3]-[5],[21],[22]), and the novelty differentiation is somewhat overstated.

The writing is dense with long strings of percentage-change statistics that make it hard to extract the core takeaways, and several key design choices (e.g., why only one CoT prompt variant, why 500 images total split unevenly across three risk levels) are not well justified.

strengths: Identifies a novel, timely, and societally important privacy risk category (inference-time location leakage from user images via MLRM reasoning) that is distinct from prior training-data privacy leakage research and grounded in a real documented harm (the Ena Matsuoka stalking case).

Introduces DOXBENCH, a carefully constructed, high-resolution, real-world dataset spanning three well-motivated privacy risk levels (including a novel 'Mirror' reflection category), addressing clear limitations of prior benchmarks that rely on low-resolution Street View images or benign landmark/tourist content.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 11 diverse models (open- and closed-source MLRMs and MLLMs) across multiple axes: VRR, error distance, hierarchical administrative accuracy, and the newly proposed GLARE metric.

GLARE is a thoughtfully derived, information-theoretic metric that jointly captures both the propensity to answer and the precision of the answer, with a clear mathematical derivation (including a flat-earth approximation justification) provided in the appendix.

Strong mechanistic analysis of root causes: human/LLM-judge verification of clue-based reasoning, CoT ablations showing transferability of reasoning patterns to MLLMs, and CLUEMINER for systematically cataloging the visual clue categories driving leakage, including explicitly privacy-sensitive clues (license plates, address numbers, etc.).

GEOMINER offers a concrete, realistic collaborative attack framework showing that leakage can be amplified even without advanced agentic capability, which strengthens the paper's real-world relevance.
Includes a human-model comparison study demonstrating models substantially outperform non-expert humans, contextualizing the practical severity of the threat.

Thorough defense discussion (image perturbation, prompt-based refusal, guardrail models) that honestly reports the limited effectiveness of current mitigations, which is a valuable negative result for the community.
Reasonable ethical framing: self-collected/staged images by researchers rather than scraping real users' social media content, reducing certain privacy/ethical concerns of the study itself.
weaknesses: Dataset and sub-study sample sizes are fairly small in several places (46 mirror images, 30-sample reasoning-pattern analysis, 30-image human comparison, only 5 human participants), which limits statistical robustness and generalizability of some claims.
Geographic scope is restricted to California; it is unclear how well findings generalize to other countries, architectural styles, sign languages, or urban/rural contexts.

Images are self-collected and partly staged by the researchers (posed selfies, deliberately composed privacy-sensitive scenes) rather than sampled from authentic user-generated social media content, which may not fully capture the diversity and noise of real-world attacker inputs.

CLUEMINER relies on models' self-reported CoT clue lists as ground truth for what clues were 'used,' which risks capturing post-hoc rationalization rather than the model's actual internal reasoning process (a known CoT faithfulness concern not discussed).

GLARE, while novel, embeds several approximations (geometric mean of median/mean error, flat-earth area approximation, uniform land prior) whose practical validity as a proxy for real privacy risk is asserted rather than empirically validated against human risk perception.

Limited statistical reporting (no confidence intervals/variance) across the large Table 1 results, making it hard to assess the significance of many reported differences between models and prompting strategies.

The paper ultimately shows that no tested defense (perturbation, prompting, guardrail) is effective, leaving the central practical contribution mostly diagnostic rather than offering a viable mitigation, though this is acknowledged as future work.

Dual-use/responsible disclosure considerations could be discussed more explicitly, since the paper effectively documents and packages an attack methodology (GEOMINER) alongside the vulnerability disclosure.
